source_title: ICC Docket 257/259-A, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement (1974)

corrected_summary: The 1836 Comancheria bounds are an encyclopedia paraphrase (Kansapedia) with no primary source. Show only as an approximate asserted-homeland layer. For SE Colorado, the KCA tribes alleged aboriginal possession of Royce 478 before the ICC; that claim was settled by compromise, not adjudicated.
notes: Quote is the plaintiffs' allegation as summarized in the settlement findings, not an ICC finding of aboriginal title. ICC dockets do not address the 1836 extent. Kavanagh (Comanche Political History) would be the scholarly check; not in library.

source_title: Treaty with the Comanche and Witchetaw Indians, Camp Holmes, Aug. 24, 1835
source_quote: free permission to hunt and trap in the Great Prairie west of the Cross Timber, to the western limits of the United States
corrected_summary: The Comanche were not simply "never asked": at Camp Holmes in 1835 they signed a treaty with the US and with removed Cherokee, Muscogee, Choctaw, Osage, Seneca and Quapaw delegates that gave all parties hunting rights west of the Cross Timbers. No recorded 1830s Comanche objection to removal was found. The treaty ceded no Comanche land.
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty with the Comanche, Witchetaw, etc., Aug. 24, 1835, 7 Stat. 474; Kappler II 435 (pagination in library OCR: 322-323)
notes: "Never asked" is the K1 pass gloss and is overstated. Do not map.

Needs Hugh McLeod to Mirabeau Lamar, Mar. 20, 1840 (Council House Fight report), printed in Winfrey, Texas Indian Papers vol. 1 (1959). Searched archive.org; no full-text copy; not in library. Standard histories agree about 12 chiefs killed. Not a land claim; keep off map.

source_title: Fitzpatrick report on Fort Atkinson treaty, 1853, as quoted in Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa (1898)

notes: Fitzpatrick describes negotiating with "the chiefs" and their refusals; nothing on how signers were selected. The selection claim is the author's conjecture ("we could assume"). Do not map.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa (1898), quoting a correspondent's report of Satanta's Medicine Lodge speech
source_quote: I have heard that you intend to settle us on a reservation near the mountains. I don't want to settle.
corrected_summary: Satanta's refusal to settle on a reservation is documented in a contemporary press report quoted by Mooney. Ten Bears' speech was not found in the library. "Preordained" is the PSL author's interpretation.

Article texts confirmed in 15 Stat. 581 (round 2). Mooney 1898 prints only speech excerpts. "Fabrications" is the author's word; do not map as fact.

source_title: ARCIA 1892, Report of Kiowa, Comanche and Wichita Agency
source_quote: The riding police have been dutifully watching for trespassers, horse" thieves, and other depredators.
notes: Kiowa agency reports for 1892, 1894, 1896, 1897, 1898 and 1899 (library reports/) record grazing leases and police patrols but no mass settler rush or large-scale theft of stone, timber or minerals. Reservation stayed closed until the Aug. 6, 1901 proclamation (ICC 4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 95). Do not map the "thousands of settlers" claim.

corrected_summary: Under the 1900 Act (Jerome Agreement) the US took 2,033,583 acres free of Indian title, granted 225,953 acres to Oklahoma for schools and sold 1,807,630 acres to homestead entrymen. It reserved 480,000 acres of tribal pasture, 100,000 acres of which were later allotted. The 50,000-settler figure and the 65 and 93 percent loss figures were not found in primary sources.

corrected_summary: Colorado received sections 16 and 36 of every township for schools under the 1875 Enabling Act; secondary sources put the original grant near 4.5 million acres (later holdings about 3 million surface acres). That KCA gained nothing from railroad or school grants is PSL's argument.
notes: Enabling Act PDF not retrievable from govinfo (pre-1951 volume path failed). Railroad grant claim not checked. No source quote copied (web search summary only).

source_title: Great Outdoors Colorado Board, December 2025 meeting minutes
source_quote: GOCO does not currently recognize the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe as an entity eligible to receive funding as identified in Article XXVII of the Colorado Constitution
corrected_summary: Tribes are not among the entities GOCO recognizes as eligible under Colo. Const. art. XXVII, but GOCO's board can and in December 2025 did use discretionary authority to fund the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe. "Bars tribal nations" overstates it. The USFS "over 200 unprotected sacred sites" figure was not found.
corrected_instrument_cite: Colo. Const. art. XXVII; GOCO Board Policy 2.11(E)
notes: USFS figure has no source in the book; would need a USFS Rocky Mountain Region statement.

source_title: Hornaday, The Extermination of the American Bison (1889)
source_cite: Hornaday 1889, Report of the National Museum 1887, p. 492, 504
source_quote: The number of individuals in the southern herd in the year 1871 must have been at least three millions
corrected_summary: Hornaday estimated the southern herd at no fewer than three million in 1871 and about four million buffalo south of the Platte around 1870, not five million. The dollar value is PSL's own calculation and differs within the book ($46 billion vs $48 billion).

source_title: Indian Reorganization Act, June 18, 1934, sec. 13; Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act, June 26, 1936
source_quote: shall not apply to the following-named Indian tribes, the members of
corrected_summary: The IRA excluded Kiowa, Comanche, Apache and other Oklahoma tribes from sections 2, 4, 7, 16, 17 and 18, not from the whole act; section 1 (no further allotment) was not on the excluded list. The 1936 OIWA (49 Stat. 1967) gave Oklahoma tribes rights to organize and to have land taken in trust; its text has no allotment-ending clause. The Mar. 20, 1934 Collier meeting and the 1950s termination account were not checked.
notes: Collier meeting needs the Anadarko congress record (NARA RG 75, Wheeler-Howard Act files).

source_title: Treaty with the Eastern Shoshoni, Fort Bridger, July 2, 1863, Art. 4
source_quote: the north Park or Buffalo House; and on the south,
corrected_summary: Primary text supports Shoshone-described limits reaching North Park and the Yampa River in 1863. The AD 1300 occupation date and pre-1800 extent rest on J. Donald Hughes via a Peter Faris article (secondary of secondary) and were not checked.
notes: Hughes, American Indians in Colorado (1977), not in library. Label pre-1800 extent as scholarly estimate.

Needs F.W. Lander, report on the Eastern Snakes (1859-60), printed in Report upon the Pacific Wagon Roads, Sen. Ex. Doc. 42, 36th Cong., 1st Sess. (1860) and in ARCIA 1859/1860. archive.org has only the title page and maps for the wagon-road report; ARCIA 1859 and 1860 djvu texts not available (usindianaffairs59/60 ids fail). Generally consistent with 1863 Art. 4.

Needs the House resolution of Feb. 14, 1855 ordering extra copies of the Pacific Railroad Survey reports (Congressional Globe / House Journal, 33d Cong., 2d Sess.) and Reports of Explorations and Surveys vol. II (1855); neither found as full text on archive.org in this pass. Surveys themselves are well documented; "illegal mapping" is the author's word (no treaty barred surveys). Do not map.

source_title: ARCIA 1863 (Commissioner Dole); Treaty with Northwestern Bands of Shoshoni, Box Elder, July 30, 1863
source_quote: Much credit is due to General Connor and the forces under his command, for their prompt and efficient services in chastising these Indians
corrected_summary: Bear River (Jan. 29, 1863) was carried out by Col. Connor's California Volunteers; the Commissioner credited Connor with forcing the bands to sue for peace. A treaty did follow: at Box Elder, July 30, 1863, the northwestern bands assented to the Fort Bridger treaty; it ceded no land. That Brigham Young took control of the land through the massacre is PSL's interpretation.
notes: LDS settlement of Cache Valley and the Washakie, Utah sale not checked (Madsen 1985).

Needs the Union Pacific-Brigham Young grading contract of May 21, 1868 (Union Pacific Railroad Museum / LDS Church History Library, Brigham Young Office Files); not online in the library. 1863 Fort Bridger Art. 3 already consented to a railway, so the contract did not precede Shoshone consent to a railroad.

Needs the map images: Doty map in the ratified treaty file for July 2, 1863 (NARA RG 11, T494/M668), O. Stewart 1957 map, Robertson 2023 overlay. Map files are not text and were not reachable. Note 1868 Art. II relinquished all territory outside the reservation, so map differences do not by themselves show unceded land.

source_title: United States v. Shoshone Tribe, 304 U.S. 111 (1938)
source_quote: No. 668. Argued March 31, April 1, 1938.-Decided April 25, 1938.
corrected_summary: The cited "Court of Claims No. H-129 (decided Dec 2, 1938)" does not match: the Supreme Court decided the Shoshone valuation case on Apr. 25, 1938 (No. 668) on review of 85 Ct. Cls. 331. Undelivered goods, school funds and the 1910 bribery claim are the author's impressions, unsourced.
notes: Bribery claim needs ARCIA 1910-1911 Shoshone agency reports (1910 text in library is partial). Winnemucca quote concerns Northern Paiute, not Eastern Shoshone.

source_title: Shoshone Tribe v. United States, 299 U.S. 476 (1937); Agreement of Apr. 21, 1896
source_quote: he treated the two tribes as equal beneficiaries of the reservation
corrected_summary: The 1896 agreement was made jointly with the Shoshone and Arapahoe tribes and paid $60,000 to both, but the Supreme Court found the Commissioner had treated the tribes as equal beneficiaries since the Arapaho were settled there on Mar. 18, 1878, over Shoshone protest. Stamm's claim that 1896 first made them equal partners, and that the Arapaho came with Shoshone consent, is not supported.
notes: Compensation in the 1930s: 299 U.S. 476 and 304 U.S. 111 (1937-38).

The 1905 promise of an irrigation system for the Indians is confirmed (33 Stat. 1016, Art. IV; round 2). The 1919 Riverton Project financing claim needs the Indian appropriation act for FY1920 (Act of June 30, 1919, 41 Stat. 3) and Reclamation Service annual report 1919-20; not in library and govinfo pre-1951 statute PDFs did not resolve in this pass.

Interlocutory award $533,013.60 less offsets; final order Apr. 22, 1957 awarded $433,013.60 after $100,000 offsets (6 Ind. Cl. Comm. 636). Single-source GIS comparison (Robertson, Mato Ohitika Analytics 2023), unpublished; and the Doty map in NARA RG 11. Neither reachable. Even if Doty's map shows more, 1868 Art. II relinquished all lands outside the reservation; do not map as unceded.

source_quote: accommodate access to and ceremonial use of Indian sacred sites by Indian religious practitioners
corrected_summary: EO 13007 citation confirmed. The rock art, medicine wheel, Tarnesse identification and Washakie visits were not checked. Browns Park NWR is a USFWS refuge; Vermillion Canyon is largely BLM land, not "BLM as a National Wildlife Refuge".
notes: Cultural claims would need BLM Little Snake Field Office cultural reports.

source_title: Great Outdoors Colorado Board, December 2025 meeting minutes
source_quote: Exercise its discretionary authority to award funding to the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe
corrected_summary: Tribes are not recognized as eligible entities under Colo. Const. art. XXVII, but the GOCO board has discretionary authority to fund them and used it in Dec. 2025. The recommendation stands as policy advice; the USFS 200-site figure is unsourced.
notes: Same source as PSL-KCA-B-029.

source_title: ARCIA 1896, Report of Shoshone Agency
source_quote: In April last Inspector McLaughlin concluded a treaty with the Shoshones and Arapahoes for the cession of the Big Horn Hot Springs
notes: The 1896 agent report records the cession but gives no reason tied to loss of Big Horn Basin hunting to ranches. Stamm's account; McLaughlin's council proceedings (Sen. Doc. 247, 54th Cong., 1st Sess.) would be the decisive source and were not found. Not mappable.

source_title: ARCIA 1863, Gov. Evans report (Colorado Superintendency)
source_quote: the chiefs of his band who visited Washington last spring, having secured the result
corrected_summary: A Tabeguache delegation did visit Washington in spring 1863 and no treaty was made there; the treaty followed at Conejos on Oct. 7, 1863. Evans described the delegates as chiefs and headmen of Head's band. That Head packed the delegation with men without standing, and that it refused to negotiate without consulting the bands, was not found in ARCIA 1863.
notes: PSL itself hedges ("Supposedly"). NARA RG 75 Colorado Superintendency letters (M234) would settle the packing claim.

source_quote: recently returned from their visit to Washington, who told their brethren that
notes: The gold-for-copper speech does not appear in ARCIA 1863; the official account says returning delegates urged peace. Speaker and record unidentified. Do not map as a quote.

source_cite: M-37051, n. 9 (citing Hayt v. United States, 38 Ct. Cl. 455, 460-465 (1903))
source_quote: Mexican law did not consider "aboriginal title" of any particular Indian group beyond a right of occupancy within their accustomed territories.
notes: This is the federal legal position, not a finding about Ute tenure. Label as such on the map. Hayt itself not fetched.

source_title: Greiner to Calhoun, Taos, Oct. 20, 1851 (postscript)
source_cite: Abel, Official Correspondence of James S. Calhoun (1915) p. 438
source_quote: preparations are being made by the Citizens of this Valley & others, to settle the lands claimed by the Eutaws in the Valley of the Los Conejos.
corrected_summary: Greiner wrote that citizens were preparing to settle lands "claimed by the Eutaws" in the Conejos valley, and that the Utes had repeatedly driven Mexicans off and would not give it up quietly. The Utes forced to retreat (to Ojo Caliente) after Kiowa and Arapaho raids were a band near Red River, not the Conejos lands. PSL's quote is altered.
notes: Planned settlement of Conejos before any Ute cession is confirmed.

Needs ARCIA 1855 (New Mexico Superintendency, Meriwether) or Meriwether correspondence for the post-council smallpox deaths; ARCIA 1854 (library arcia-annualreportcom48unkngoog.txt) predates it and ARCIA 1855 djvu not available on archive.org. Deliberate infection: PSL itself says unclear; do NOT map.
Needs Manypenny letter of Jan. 30, 1855 (NARA RG 75, Letters Sent, M21) and the El Pueblo depredation claim files; not digitized in library. The Pueblo attack itself is not disputed.

Needs Fauntleroy's report of Apr. 1855 in the Secretary of War annual report (Sen. Ex. Doc. 1, 34th Cong., 1st Sess., pt. 2); archive.org search found no full text. "Probably placed as slaves" is PSL's hedge; do not map captives' fate as fact.

source_title: Treaty with the Mohuache Band of Utahs, Sept. 11, 1855, and Meriwether to Manypenny, Sept. 15, 1855 (unratified)
source_cite: Unratified treaty, Sept. 11, 1855, Art. III (Avalon Project)
source_quote: These Indians did not appear to be in so destitute a condition as the Jicarillas
corrected_summary: The Mouache treaty was signed Sept. 11, 1855 (not August) and ceded all Mouache claims in New Mexico except a reservation (Art. III); it was never ratified. Meriwether reported the Mouaches less destitute than the Jicarillas, though they had lost many people and horses. The mule-eating detail and the settler petition to Pierce were not found.
corrected_instrument_cite: Unratified Treaty with the Mohuache Utahs, Sept. 11, 1855 (NARA T494)
notes: HTML file; quote matches after tag stripping. Capote treaty date (Aug. 1855) not checked.
Needs ARCIA 1859 (Supt. J.L. Collins, New Mexico); not available as text on archive.org (usindianaffairs59usdorich fails). "Last and only hunting region" is PSL's characterization; do not map.

source_title: ARCIA 1868, Gov. A.C. Hunt (Colorado Superintendency)
source_quote: the concluding of a new treaty, entirely acceptable to the Indians themselves
notes: The contemporaneous official account calls the 1868 treaty acceptable to all bands. No primary source checked supports "forced to relinquish" or hotel-room coercion; the treaty text does not designate Ouray head chief. Coercion stays unattributed; do not map.

Band organization is standard ethnography (Stewart; Simmons, The Ute Indians of Utah, Colorado, and New Mexico, 2000) not in library. "Five attempts on Ouray's life" unsourced; ARCIA 1868-1880 searched for Ouray, no such count. Do not map.

source_title: ARCIA 1866: Carson to Gov. Cummings, Fort Garland, Oct. 7, 1866
source_quote: war, with Cuneatch's band at least, has commenced. Yesterday Ulay came to this post to see me ; he says he will not fight.
corrected_summary: In early October 1866 Kaniache's Mouache band fought troops near Trinidad, and Ouray went to Fort Garland and told Carson he would not fight. Governor Cummings called the outbreak "wholly inexplicable"; the murder of Kaniache's son as cause was not found in ARCIA 1866-1868.
notes: Son's murder needs Fort Garland or Colorado newspaper sources.

Schurz's "more and more precarious" statement not in ARCIA 1879-1881. Needs H.R. Rep. No. 1401 (46th Cong., 2d Sess., 1880) or Secretary of Interior annual report 1879; not in library. Framing is PSL's.

source_title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa (1898), on the Adobe Walls fight
source_quote: seventy-two Ute and Jicarilla Apache Indians, was under command of
corrected_summary: Ute and Jicarilla scouts (72) served with Carson against the Kiowa and Comanche at Adobe Walls, Nov. 25, 1864. Ute service in the 1863 Navajo campaign was not checked here (Official Records ser. I vol. 26 not in library). "Divide and conquer" is PSL's characterization.

notes: Legend-level claim with no source. Spanish San Juan mining would need Rivera expedition diaries (1765) or Baker 1860 party accounts. Do not map.

Needs the unnamed Colorado newspaper, Nov. 1873 (Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection, search "Little Annie" Adams); coloradohistoricnewspapers.org returned HTTP 403 to this agent. Not in ARCIA 1873. Keep off map.

source_title: ARCIA 1871, G.F. Jocknick special report on Colorado agencies, Sept. 30, 1871
source_quote: gives unmistakable evidence of honesty and integrity
corrected_summary: The 1871 investigator (Jocknick) recorded Ute complaints that Agent Trask refused rations when they were starving, but found Trask's confused accounts showed honesty and attributed the shortage to supplies still in transit. He mentions no $25,000 held in a Denver bank; the only $25,000 in the report is the estimated cost of surveying the reservation lines.
notes: Ration complaint is real and can be cited as a Ute complaint; the bank claim should not appear.

source_title: ARCIA 1875, Los Pinos agent H.F. Bond
source_quote: They now declare that they will not receive any compensation until the boundary-line is settled.
corrected_summary: Bond reported general Ute dissatisfaction with the Brunot agreement, refusal to accept the delayed compensation until the boundary was settled, and insistence they never meant to sell farming lands. ARCIA 1874 shows the Weeminuche and Capote still living at Abiquiu in New Mexico. A specific southern-band accusation that the Tabeguache manipulated them was not found.
notes: Settle the southern-band accusation with the Abiquiu and Cimarron agency reports 1875-76 (not in library).

source_title: Testimony in relation to the Ute Indian Outbreak, H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess. (1880)
source_cite: H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, testimony of Henry James (Ute) and C.B. Fisk
source_quote: Those Indians who lived near Mr. Meeker would receive rations, but Jack's people and those Indians who lived some distance off would not receive rations.
corrected_summary: Ute witness Henry James testified that Jack's people and Utes living farther off did not get rations, while Josephine Meeker testified rations were only increased for those who worked. Fisk testified the Indian Office itself appointed Meeker. A Pitkin-Teller-Evans-Byers placement plan was not found in this record; that thesis is PSL's.
notes: Not mappable.

source_title: ARCIA 1879: Pitkin telegram of July 5, 1879; Crook indorsement Aug. 4, 1879
source_quote: besides killing the game the Indians committed no depredations
corrected_summary: Pitkin's July 5, 1879 telegram did claim "millions of dollars of timber" burned and urged removal to Indian Territory. Thornburgh's inquiry, forwarded by Gen. Crook, found the Indians committed no depredations besides killing game. But Agent Meeker himself reported his Indians burning timber, and some settlers (e.g. A.H. Smart) blamed Utes for fires, so the record is contested.
notes: Telegram text: "They have already burned millions of dollars of timber". Not mappable.

source_title: Testimony in relation to the Ute Indian Outbreak (1880); ARCIA 1879 Meeker telegram Sept. 10, 1879
source_cite: H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., p. 158 and testimony of Charles Adams
source_quote: at the crossing of Milk Creek, right at the line of the reservation as we then understood it
corrected_summary: Meeker's plowing of contested pasture and his Sept. 10 telegram reporting assault by Johnson (Canalla) are confirmed. The battle was at the Milk Creek crossing on the reservation line, and Adams testified the Utes saw Thornburgh's advance as bad faith after he first agreed to meet halfway. That Meeker's assault claim was false is not established by these sources.
notes: Not a land claim.

source_title: Testimony of Gov. Frederick Pitkin, H.R. Misc. Doc. 38 (1880)
source_cite: H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., p. 113
source_quote: I sent Mnjor-General Cook, of the State militia, on a special train from Denver to relieve that point
corrected_summary: Pitkin did send Colorado militia (Maj. Gen. D.J. Cook) to Lake City and other points after the Milk Creek fight. No order to kill all Indians found off the reservation appears in his testimony or ARCIA 1879-1880.
notes: Kill-order claim needs Pitkin's Oct. 1879 militia orders (Colorado State Archives, Adjutant General records); not online. Do not map the order. OCR reads "Mnjor-General".

source_title: Testimony of Charles Adams, H.R. Misc. Doc. 38 (1880)
source_cite: H.R. Misc. Doc. 38, 46th Cong., 2d Sess., p. 3-6
source_quote: I thereupon wrote the dispatch to the Secretary that the women had been given up and no indignities had been offered to them.
corrected_summary: Adams first reported no indignities, then examined the women under oath in Greeley, where they testified to sexual assault. The commission demanded 12 men: 4 named by the women for assault and the massacre, and 8 the women saw armed before the fight and plundering afterwards, not seen killing. Adams says he went to Greeley after consulting Ouray, with the Secretary's approval; meetings with Pitkin driving it were not found.
notes: Sensitive; keep off map.
Needs Colorado House Journal, 3d General Assembly (1881), H.B. 178; not found on archive.org in this pass. PSL does not say it passed; do not imply enactment.

source_title: ARCIA 1884, Southern Ute Agency report (Agent Warren Patten)
source_quote: there was an attack made on Indians by cattle-men about 20 miles west of the reservation line
corrected_summary: The agent reported a July 1884 attack by cattlemen on Indians about 20 miles west of the reservation (in Utah); the cattlemen said they were Southern Utes holding many of their horses, and the Utes said the raiders were renegades. Seizure of horses from pass-holders, a Ute man shot, and pursuit by the 6th Cavalry with about 80 volunteers were not in ARCIA 1884.
notes: Location is in Utah (outside Colorado cessions). OCR "clain ing".

source_title: ARCIA 1887, Commissioner's report on the Colorow affair
source_quote: The Indian loss in this fight is said to be one man, two small girls, and an infant boy killed
corrected_summary: The 1887 posse (Game Warden Burgett, Sheriff Kendall) burned Colorow's camp, including property of Chipeta; militia under Maj. Leslie and the posse then attacked the camp at dawn near the reservation line. The Commissioner reported four Utes killed (one man, two small girls, an infant boy), not eight, and losses of over 600 horses and nearly 2,500 sheep and goats.
notes: Commissioner calls it attack "without warning" on "unsuspecting and defenseless" party: that characterization is the Commissioner's.

source_title: ARCIA 1907, "The Absentee Utes"; ARCIA 1908
source_quote: a band of about 200 nonprogressive Utes
corrected_summary: In 1906 a band of about 200 (the Wyoming governor said 300) mostly White River Utes left Uintah for Pine Ridge after allotment and the opening of their surplus lands. At Wyoming's governor's request troops took them to Fort Meade, then the Cheyenne River Reservation; 360 returned to Utah with Capt. Johnson in 1908. "About 400" and an alliance aim are not in ARCIA.
notes: OCR "nonprogressive Utes" split across line (stripped match). Not a land claim.

source_title: ICC Docket 349, Findings of Fact on the Stipulated Settlement (Feb. 18, 1965)
source_cite: ICC Docket 349, 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707, Findings 1, 4
source_quote: had no obligation to furnish such a reservation
corrected_summary: In Docket 349 the Uncompahgre claim was that the US never gave them a reservation in Colorado or Utah as the 1880 agreement required; the US denied any such obligation. The case ended in a compromise settlement, a net $300,000 judgment after offsets, entered Feb. 18, 1965. It is a settlement, not a finding that the US failed its obligation.
corrected_instrument_cite: ICC Docket 349, 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 707, 728 (1965); 21 Stat. 199
notes: Claimed offsets were $686,500 to $1,180,721 (Finding 15).

source_title: ICC Docket 327, Findings of Fact Part 2 (Sept. 14, 1962)

source_quote: The Commission finds that, as of April 29, 1874, Royce Area 566 had a fair market value in the amount of $8,500,000.00.
corrected_instrument_cite: ICC Docket 327, 11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 180, 222 (1962); final judgment 14 Ind. Cl. Comm. 706 (1965)
notes: The $40,773,533 figure was the petitioner's experts' (Vandervilt and Parker) value of the mineral lands (11 Ind. Cl. Comm. 180, Finding 35). $507,662.84 credited as consideration; held unconscionable (Finding 53). PSL's 1962 date is right for the valuation; final judgment Feb. 18, 1965 for $7,908,586.16. "Probably more accurate" is PSL opinion.

source_title: ICC Docket 328, Findings of Fact (May 6, 1966)
source_cite: ICC Docket 328, 17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 28, Finding 14; final order 26 Ind. Cl. Comm. 10 (1971)
source_quote: No interest was paid on any part of the money deposited in the fund
notes: Fund "Indian Moneys, Proceeds of Labor, Southern Ute Indians", $19,124.22 deposited 1892-1940 (ICC finding, not only the tribe's claim). The opinion (17 Ind. Cl. Comm. 42) ordered a further accounting; case dismissed with prejudice July 1971 as barred by res judicata after 402 U.S. 159.

source_title: ARCIA 1865, Head to Evans, July 17, 1865
source_quote: in future no more captives are to be purchased or sold
notes: Head inventoried Navajo and Ute captives held in Conejos and Costilla counties in 1865 and announced a ban on sales. Whether he himself held or traded captives needs his enclosed captive list (NARA RG 75, M234, Colorado Superintendency 1865), which ARCIA does not print. Attribute the claim to TREC only.
